title: Colorado OAC Workers' Compensation Decision — WC 5-266-262-004
text:
Office of Administrative Courts
State of Colorado
Workers’ Compensation No. WC 5-266-262-004
Issues
Whether Respondents have established by a preponderance of the evidence that
⮚
Claimant did not sustain a compensable injury, entitling Respondents to withdraw
their General Admission of Liability (GAL).
If Respondents fail to establish grounds for withdrawal of their GAL, whether
⮚
Claimant has proven by a preponderance of the evidence that Tezspire is
medical treatment that is reasonable, and necessary to cure or relieve the effects
of an industrial injury.
Whether Respondents are liable for Claimant’s outstanding balance of $6,358.64
⮚
for prescriptions through Injured Workers Pharmacy.
Findings of Fact
1. Claimant works for Respondent, an energy service company. On December 12,
2023, Claimant, in the course of his employment with Employer, opened a crate
that contained metal cylinders containing bromine trifluoride (BT), a chemical
Employer uses for cutting pipes. As Claimant opened the crate, he was exposed
to fumes from a leaking cylinder, believed to be BT, for approximately fifteen
seconds. At the time, Claimant was not wearing respiratory protection. Claimant
testified that he immediately experienced shortness of breath and tightness in his
chest and lungs. He indicated that his symptoms progressed over the day, and it
became difficult to establish a normal breathing pattern.
2. On December 15, 2023, Claimant sought treatment at UC Health’s Occupational
Medicine Clinic in Greeley, under the care of Oscar Sanders, M.D. He reported
that he had inhaled BT and felt instant dizziness with lightheadedness. Claimant
reported that since the incident, he had begun to experience tightness in his
chest, difficulty taking deep breaths, some mental confusion and being unable to
1

focus. Claimant’s examination was noted to be unremarkable; he declined
inhalers or other treatment and was scheduled for follow up in two weeks. He
was advised to wear a mask at all times but otherwise given no work restrictions.
3. Claimant returned to UCH on December 29, 2023 reporting no improvement. He
continued to experience shortness of breath, and right lateral chest tightness.
Claimant was then referred to UCH Pulmonology for evaluation.
4. On January 8, 2024, Claimant saw Elvira Aguila, M.D., at the UCH pulmonology
clinic, on referral from Dr. Sanders. He continued to report shortness of breath,
worse with cold air exposure. Dr. Aguila noted that Claimant was using Albuterol
occasionally with positive results. Claimant’s pulmonary function testing and
chest x-rays were normal. Dr. Aguila recommended a methacholine challenge
test (MCT) to rule out reactive airways dysfunction syndrome (RADS). The MCT
was performed on January 24, 2024. Dr. Aguila indicated that the MCT confirmed
RADS, likely secondary to chemical inhalation exposure at work. She started
Claimant on Advair and prescribed a prednisone burst.
5. Over the following months, Claimant continued to receive treatment at UCH,
through ATP Oscar Sanders, M.D., and the UCH pulmonology clinic. During this
time, Claimant reported some improvement in his breathing symptoms but
continued persistent chest tightness. In his report of February 19, 2024, Dr.
Sanders noted that he had reviewed medical literature indicating that inhalation
of BT may result in bronchospasm and air way hyperactivity. He was diagnosed
with moderate persistent occupational asthma and moderate persistent reactive
airways dysfunction syndrome (RADS), with a history of toxin inhalation
exposure.
6. On April 8, 2024, Respondents filed a General Admission of Liability (GAL)
admitting liability for medical and temporary total disability benefits.
7. In May 2024, a chest CT was performed which was negative, except for bilateral
lower lobe air trapping “which can be seen with small airways disease.” At a
follow up visit, Dr. Aguila noted that the presence of air trapping on the CT was
2

consistent with Claimant’s airway disease and prescribed a second prednisone
burst.
8. In June 2024, Claimant began evaluation and treatment with Karin Pacheco,
M.D, at National Jewish Health Occupational Medicine Clinic on referral from Dr.
Sanders. Dr. Pacheco diagnosed Claimant occupational asthma/ RADS and
constrictive bronchiolitis, caused by exposure to bromine trifluoride, as well as an
abnormal breathing pattern caused by trapped lung volume.
9. In August 2024, Claimant underwent a cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET),
which is a ramp test performed on a stationary bicycle. Claimant stopped the test
due to lower extremity fatigue and numbness in his hands. The pulmonologist
who reviewed the CPET results, Kevin Rurak, M.D., noted that there was no
physiologic limitation to Claimant continuing the exercise test, having ample heart
rate and ventilatory capacity. Dr. Rurak commented that there were abnormalities
contributing to the Claimant’s exercise limitations, including cardiac
abnormalities, blunted heart rate response (although Claimant’s heart rate and
oxygen levels were out of proportion to the VO2 achieved), and ventilatory
abnormalities included an abnormal pattern of ventilatory recruitment. Dr. Rurak
indicated that Claimant’s test results were potentially due to an abnormal
breathing pattern and hyperventilation with respiratory alkalosis. He noted that
Claimant had an abnormal and inefficient breathing strategy, which likely
contributed to the results.
10.Claimant reported similar symptoms of increased shortness of breath and tingling
in his hands with exercise during exercise physiology appointments at UCH in
September 2024.
11.Over the following year, Claimant remained under the care of Dr. Pacheco and
Dr. Sanders, and reported consistent symptoms of chest tightness, and difficulty
breathing. Claimant’s treatment consisted of high dose inhaled steroids and long
and short acting bronchodilators, speech therapy, and respiratory therapy.
12.In August 2025, Dr. Pacheco prescribed a six-month course of treatment with
Tezspire, a biologic medication. At hearing, Dr. Pacheco testified that Tezspire
was a reasonable treatment for both asthma and smaller airways disease, and
3

that the purpose of the medication is to treat Claimant’s shortness of breath and
increase his exercise capacity. She noted if Claimant had no response to the
medication she would consider him to have reached maximum medical
improvement (MMI). Insurer denied authorization of Tezspire.
13.On September 16, 2025, Dr. Sanders prescribed Claimant Spiriva Respimat and
budesonide formoterol (Symbicort) as needed for maintenance therapy for
asthma with eleven refills of Spiriva through September 15, 2026, and Symbicort
until discontinued. Claimant filled the Spiriva prescription through Injured
Workers Pharmacy (IWP) on September 16, 2025, and received refills on
December 10, 2025, January 8, 2026, February 9, 2026, February 10, 2026,
March 10, 2026, and April 8, 2026. Claimant’s medical records indicate that he
continued to use Spiriva during this time, and Dr. Sanders continued to
recommend it for treatment of work-related asthma.
14.Claimant also filled his prescription for Symbicort through IWP on September 16,
2025, December 10, 2025, January 8, 2026, February 9, 2026, March 10, 2026,
April 8, 2026. Claimant’s medical records indicate that he continued to use
Symbicort, in conjunction with Spiriva during this time, and Dr. Sanders
continued to recommend it for treatment of his work-related asthma.
15.Dr. Sanders prescribed Claimant daily Candesartan on March 30, 2026.
Claimant’s medical records contain no information regarding the reasons for this
prescription or the relationship to Claimant’s work injury. Dr. Sanders’ record
from March 30, 2026 states “start Candesartan daily – monitor home BP,” with no
further explanation.
16.During the pendency of the claim, Respondents engaged Carlos Cebrian, M.D.,
to perform medical record reviews on several occasions. Dr. Cebrian issued
reports dated February 21, 2025, September 5, 2025, and April 2, 2026. As
relevant to the issues before the ALJ, in his February 21, 2025 report, Dr.
Cebrian indicated it was his “medically probably opinion that the initial exposure
to bromine resulted in a respiratory condition consistent with reactive airway
disease that required treatment under the 12/12/2023 claim.” Although Dr.
Cebrian believed that Claimant’s ongoing respiratory complaints were “poorly
4

explained” and may not be related to the initial exposure, he reiterated that in his
September 5, 2025 report, that he believed Claimant sustained an injury from the
work-related BT exposure that required treatment.
17.On December 10, 2025, Claimant saw Jeffrey Schwartz, M.D., for a Respondent-
sponsored IME. Dr. Schwartz testified at hearing consistently with his report.
Based on his examination and review of records, Dr. Schwartz opined that
Claimant sustained no injury as a result of the BT exposure, and that Claimant
was “a malingerer.” In support of this position, Dr. Schwartz opined that the
Claimant’s January 24, 2024 MCT test was not properly performed, rendering the
diagnosis of RADS invalid. He further opined that Claimant’s brief exposure to BT
was insufficient to cause RADS or any other injury, and that his lack of significant
improvement is inconsistent with RADS.
18.Dr. Schwartz indicated that the Claimant’s exposure to BT was not sufficient to
cause an injury, noting that Claimant did not report irritation of his eyes or nose,
and that if Claimant’s exposure was sufficient to cause respiratory irritation, it
should have also his eyes, and nose.
19.Dr. Schwartz also took issue with Claimant’s CPET testing, indicating that
Claimant gave suboptimal effort and controlled his breathing during the test,
which resulted in an invalid CPET test.
20.Dr. Schwartz further opined that Claimant’s CT scan which showed focal air
trapping was inconsistent with constrictive bronchiolitis because the disease
typically causes diffuse trapping throughout the lungs, rather than in one location.
Ultimately, Dr. Schwartz opined that Claimant’s providers misdiagnosed him, he
sustained no work-related injury, required no medical treatment, and is
malingering.
21.Following the issuance of Dr. Schwartz’s report, Dr. Cebrian issued a
supplemental report in which he indicated that he no longer believed Claimant
sustained a work-related injury, based on Dr. Schwartz’s opinions.
22.On March 26, 2026, Dr. Pacheco authored a report regarding Claimant’s
condition, its relationship to his employment, and Dr. Schwartz’s report. Dr.
Pacheco opined that Claimant developed airways disease from BT exposure,
5

that first affected the larger airways, causing asthma. The exposure also affected
smaller airways which healed with scarring, that caused constrictive bronchiolitis.
She explained that that Claimant underwent testing that established the
diagnosis of occupational asthma/RADS, and constrictive bronchiolitis. These
tests included the February 2024 methacholine challenge which was positive for
severe bronchial hyperresponsiveness, which she indicated established the
diagnosis of occupational asthma/RADS; an April 20, 2024 chest CT, which
demonstrated air trapping consistent with constrictive bronchiolitis; August 9,
2024 pulmonary function tests which showed elevated residual volume, which
increased with bronchodilator treatment, consistent with air trapping and
constrictive bronchiolitis; and an abnormal August 12, 2024 CPET. Dr. Pacheco
indicated that she did not agree with Dr. Schwartz’s opinions concerning
Claimant’s testing, and indicated the tests were reviewed by physicians who
applied objective standard criteria. She also indicated that she did not agree with
Dr. Schwartz’s opinion that Claimant was malingering, characterizing the
assertion as unsubstantiated.
23.Dr. Pacheco indicated that Claimant had not reached MMI, because further
treatment could improve his lung function, including Tezspire which had not been
approved by insurer. She indicated that in her opinion, this treatment offered the
best chance to improve his lung function.
24.On April 9, 2026, the parties conducted the deposition of Dr. Sanders. Dr.
Sanders is Claimant’s primary authorized treating physician (ATP) and has
treated Claimant since the onset of his claim. As relevant to the issues before the
ALJ, Dr. Sanders testified that BT is a highly corrosive chemical agent that
decomposes into two different types of acid when exposed to water. When BT
comes into contact with mucous membranes, it forms oxygen-free radicals which
are damaging to tissues. Dr. Sanders testified that Claimant’s exposure to BT
was medically significant, taking into consideration that it was inhaled without
respiratory protection and the toxicity of the chemical.
25.Dr. Sanders opined that Claimant was diagnosed with occupational asthma and
RADS were related to his exposure to BT, based on the temporal relationship
6

between the onset of symptoms and exposure, and the objective testing
conducted by pulmonologists. He indicated that Claimant’s treating specialists,
including Dr. Pacheco, have recommended additional treatment that might
improve his condition, and as a result, Claimant has not reached MMI.
Conclusions of Law
Generally
A. The purpose of the Workers’ Compensation Act of Colorado, §§ 8-40-101, et
seq., C.R.S., is to assure the quick and efficient delivery of disability and medical
benefits to injured workers at a reasonable cost to employers, without the
necessity of litigation. See § 8-40-102(1), C.R.S. Claimant shoulders the burden
of proving entitlement to benefits by a preponderance of the evidence. See § 8-
43-201, C.R.S. A preponderance of the evidence is that which leads the trier-of-
fact, after considering all of the evidence, to find that a fact is more probably true
than not. Page v. Clark, 592 P.2d 792 (Colo. 1979). The facts in a workers’
compensation case must be interpreted neutrally; neither in favor of the rights of
the claimant, nor in favor of the rights of respondents; and a workers’
compensation claim shall be decided on the merits. § 8-43-201, C.R.S.
B. Assessing weight, credibility, and sufficiency of evidence in Workers'
Compensation proceedings is the exclusive domain of the administrative law
judge. University Park Care Center v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 43 P.3d 637
(Colo. App. 2001). Even if other evidence in the record may have supported a
contrary inference, it is for the ALJ to resolve conflicts in the evidence, make
credibility determinations, and draw plausible inferences from the evidence. Id. at
641. When determining credibility, the fact finder should consider, among other
things, the consistency or inconsistency of the witness's testimony and actions;
the reasonableness or unreasonableness (probability or improbability) of the
testimony and actions; the motives of the witness; whether the testimony has
been contradicted; and bias, prejudice, or interest. Prudential Ins. Co. v. Cline, 57
P.2d 1205 (Colo. 1936); Bodensieck v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 183 P.3d
684 (Colo. App. 2008). The weight and credibility to be assigned expert
7

testimony is a matter within the discretion of the ALJ. Cordova v. Indus. Claim
Appeals Office, 55 P.3d 186 (Colo. App. 2002). To the extent expert testimony is
subject to conflicting interpretations, the ALJ may resolve the conflict by crediting
part or none of the testimony. Colorado Springs Motors Ltd. v. Indus. Comm’n,
441 P.2d 21 (Colo. 1968).
C. The ALJ's factual findings concern only evidence and inferences found to be
dispositive of the issues involved; the ALJ has not addressed every piece of
evidence or every inference that might lead to conflicting conclusions and has
rejected evidence contrary to the above findings as unpersuasive. Magnetic
Eng’g, Inc. v. Indus. Claim Appeals Office, 5 P.3d 385 (Colo. App. 2000).
Withdrawal Of General Admission Of Liability
D. By filing an admission of liability and admitting for benefits, Respondents’
“admitted that the claimant has sustained the burden of proving entitlement to
benefits.” City of Brighton v. Rodriguez, 318 P.3d 496 (Colo. 2014). If
Respondents seek to withdraw the admission of liability, they must prove by a
preponderance of the evidence that Claimant did not sustain an injury that arose
out of and occurred in the course and scope of employment. See Section 8-41-
201(1), C.R.S. (“a party seeking to modify an issue determined by a general or
final admission . . . shall bear the burden of proof for any such modification.”). A
“preponderance of the evidence” is that quantum of evidence that makes a fact,
or facts, more reasonably probable, or improbable, than not. Page v. Clark, 592
P.2d 792 (1979).
E. The Workers’ Compensation Act distinguishes between the terms “accident” and
“injury.” The term “accident refers to an unexpected, unusual, or undesigned
occurrence. Section 8-40-201(1), C.R.S. However, an “injury” refers to the
physical trauma caused by the accident and is the result of an accident. City of
Boulder v. Payne, 426 P.2d 194 (1967). The mere fact that an accident occurs
does not rise to the level of compensability unless the accident results in an
injury. Leary v. Vail Resorts, Inc. W.C. No. 5-075-399-002 (ICAO, April 24, 2020).
A compensable industrial accident is one that results in an injury requiring
8

treatment or causing disability. H & H Warehouse v. Vicory, 805 P.2d 1167 (Colo.
App. 1990). The fact that medical treatment occurred does not require a finding
that medical treatment was required because of a work incident. Washburn v.
City Market, W.C. 5-109-470 (ICAO June 3, 2020).
F. Respondents have failed to establish grounds sufficient to withdraw their GAL.
The evidence is uncontroverted that Claimant was exposed to BT fumes in the
course of his employment with Employer. The primary dispute is whether the
Claimant’s exposure was sufficient to cause an injury. Dr. Schwartz testified that
Claimant’s exposure was brief, and insufficient to cause injury. As a result,
Claimant could not have sustained any injury as a result of the exposure. While
Drs. Sanders and Dr. Pacheco opined that the exposure was sufficient to cause
injury.
G. The ALJ finds that Dr. Schwartz’s opinions as to purported inconsistencies and
abnormalities in Claimant’s testing, including the MCT and CPET testing, relate
primarily to the chronicity of Claimant’s symptoms, rather than whether Claimant
sustained an injury in the first instance. Moreover, none of Claimant’s treatment
physicians indicated that Claimant’s MCT or CPET tests were “invalid” as Dr.
Schwartz opined. Dr. Aguila, in UCH’s pulmonology clinic, did not indicate any
issues with the MCT test, and opined that it was consistent with RADS. Although
Dr. Rurak indicated there were abnormalities in the CPET, he did not
characterize the results as invalid, or indicative of the level of manipulation
suggested by Dr. Schwartz. While Dr. Schwartz has opined that Claimant is a
“malingerer” no other provider has suggested such, and there is no credible
evidence in the records to indicate that Claimant has sufficient knowledge to
consciously manipulate either an MCT or CPET test. The ALJ finds Dr.
Schwartz’s opinions unpersuasive to establish that Claimant sustained no injury
as a result of his work-related BT exposure. The ALJ finds persuasive the
testimony and opinions of Drs. Pacheco and Sanders, that Claimant sustained an
injury requiring treatment as the result of his BT exposure. Respondents’ request
to withdraw their General Admission of Liability is denied.
9

Specific Medical Treatment
A. Respondents are liable to provide medical treatment that is reasonable and
necessary to cure and relieve the effects of the industrial injury. Section 8-42-
101(1)(a), C.R.S. A service is medically necessary if it cures or relieves the
effects of the injury and is directly associated with the claimant’s physical needs.
Bellone v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 940 P.2d 1116 (Colo. App. 1997); Parker v.
Iowa Tanklines, Inc., W.C. No. 4-517-537, (ICAO May 31, 2006). The question of
whether the claimant proved treatment is reasonable and necessary is one of
fact for the ALJ. Kroupa v. Indus. Claim Appeals Off., 53 P.3d 1192 (Colo. App.
2002). Hobirk v. Colorado Springs School Dist., W.C. No. 4-835-556-01 (ICAO
Nov. 15, 2012). Respondents are also liable for treatment where “employment-
related activities aggravate, accelerate, or combine with a preexisting condition to
cause a need for medical treatment.” Schoenberger v. Dillons Co., W.C. No. 4-
934-299-02 (ICAO Aug. 10, 2016). When the respondents challenge the
claimant’s request for specific medical treatment the claimant bears the burden of
proof to establish entitlement to the benefits. Martin v. El Paso School Dist., W.C.
No. 3-979-487, (ICAO Jan. 11, 2012); Ford v. Regional Transp. Dist., W.C. No.
4-309-217 (ICAO Feb. 12, 2009).
B. Claimant has established by a preponderance of the evidence that Tezspire
prescribed by Dr. Pacheco is reasonable, necessary, treatment to cure or relieve
the effects of Claimant’s industrial injury. The ALJ finds persuasive Dr. Pacheco’s
opinion that Tezspire may result in improvement of Claimant’s condition, and that
if it does not, Claimant will likely be at MMI. No credible evidence was admitted
indicating that Tezspire was an inappropriate treatment for Claimant’s condition,
other than Dr. Schwartz’s opinion that Claimant sustained no injury the ALJ has
not found credible. Claimant’s request for authorization of Tezspire is granted.
C. Claimant has established that the prescriptions for Spiriva and Symbicort are
reasonable and necessary medical treatment related to his work injury. The
record reflects that Dr. Sanders prescribed and repeatedly refilled both
medications, that Claimant has continued to use them in conjunction with one
10

another, and that Dr. Sanders has continued to recommend them for treatment of
Claimant's work-related asthma. Moreover no physician has credibly opined that
these medications are unreasonable or unnecessary treatment for Claimant's
condition; the only contrary opinions were predicated on the rejected position that
Claimant sustained no work injury. Claimant’s request for authorization of Spiriva
and Symbicort is granted.
D. Claimant has failed to establish that prescriptions for Candesartan Cilexetil are
reasonable, necessary, or related to his work injury. Claimant’s request for
authorization of Candesartan Cilexetil is denied.
Order
It is therefore ordered that:
1. Respondents request to withdraw their General Admission of Liability is denied.
2. Claimant’s request for authorization of Tezspire recommended by Dr. Pacheco is
granted.
3. Respondents are liable for payment of Claimant’s prescriptions for Spiriva and
Symbicort through IWP from September 16, 2025 to April 8, 2026.
4. Respondents are not liable for payment of Claimant’s prescriptions for
Candesartan Cilexetil.
All matters not determined herein are reserved for future determination.
NOTE: If you are dissatisfied with the ALJ's order, you may file a Petition to Review the
order with the Denver Office of Administrative Courts, 1525 Sherman St., 4th Floor,
Denver, CO 80203. You must file your Petition to Review within twenty (20) days after
mailing or service of the order, as indicated on the certificate of mailing or service;
otherwise, the ALJ's order will be final. You may file the Petition to Review by mail, as
long as the certificate of mailing attached to your petition shows: (1) That you mailed it
within twenty (20) days after mailing or service of the order of the ALJ; and (2) That you
mailed it to the above address for the Denver Office of Administrative Courts. You may
file your Petition to Review electronically by emailing the Petition to Review to the
following email address: oac-ptr@state.co.us. If the Petition to Review is emailed to the
11

aforementioned email address, the Petition to Review is deemed filed in Denver
pursuant to OACRP 27 and Section 8-43-301, C.R.S. If the Petition to Review is filed by
email to the proper email address, it does not need to be mailed to the Denver Office of
Administrative Courts. For further information regarding procedures to follow when filing
a Petition to Review, see Rule 27, OACRP. You may access a petition to review form
at: http://www.colorado.gov/dpa/oac/forms-WC.htm.

Steven R. Kabler
Administrative Law Judge
